paragraphs: Alyosha soon got to Madame Hohlakov’s house, a handsome two-story stone building, one of the finest in our town. Madame Hohlakov spent most of her time in another province, where she had an estate, or in Moscow, where she owned a house. Even so, she had a house in our town too, passed down from her ancestors. Her estate in our district was the biggest of her three, and yet until now she had spent very little time in our province. She came running out to Alyosha in the hall.
“Did you get my letter about the new miracle?” She spoke fast and nervously.
“Yes.”
“Did you show it to everyone? He gave a son back to his mother!”
“He is dying today,” said Alyosha.

“I’ve heard, I know, oh, how I long to talk to you about all this, to you or to somebody. No, to you, to you! And how sorry I am that I can’t see him! The whole town is stirred up, everyone is in suspense. But now—do you know Katerina Ivanovna is here at this very moment?”
“Ah, that’s lucky,” cried Alyosha. “Then I can see her here. She told me yesterday that I must come and see her today without fail.”

“I know, I know everything. I’ve heard exactly what happened yesterday—and the atrocious way that—creature behaved. _C’est tragique_, and if I’d been in her place I have no idea what I’d have done. And your brother Dmitri Fyodorovitch, what do you make of him?—my goodness! Alexey Fyodorovitch, I’m forgetting, just imagine it; your brother is in there with her, not that dreadful brother who was so shocking yesterday, but the other one, Ivan Fyodorovitch. He’s sitting with her, talking; they’re having a serious conversation. If you could only imagine what’s passing between them now—it’s awful, I tell you it’s lacerating, it’s like some incredible tale of horror. They’re ruining their lives for no reason that anyone can see. They both know it, and they revel in it. I’ve been watching for you! I’ve been thirsting for you! It’s too much for me, that’s the worst of it. I’ll tell you all about it in a minute, but right now I have to speak about something else, the most important thing—I’d completely forgotten what matters most. Tell me, why has Lise been in hysterics? The moment she heard you were here, she started having hysterics!”

“_Maman_, it’s you who are hysterical now, not me,” Lise’s voice rang out through a tiny crack in the side door. She sounded as if she wanted to laugh and was trying her hardest to hold it back. Alyosha noticed the crack at once, and no doubt Lise was peeping through it, but he couldn’t see her.

“And no wonder, Lise, no wonder ... your whims will make me hysterical too. But she is so ill, Alexey Fyodorovitch, she’s been so ill all night, feverish and moaning! I could hardly wait for morning and for Herzenstube to arrive. He says he can make nothing of it, that we have to wait. Herzenstube always comes and says he can make nothing of it. The minute you came near the house, she screamed, went into hysterics, and insisted that we wheel her back into this room.”
“Mamma, I didn’t know he’d come. I didn’t want to be wheeled into this room because of him.”
“That’s not true, Lise. Yulia ran to tell you that Alexey Fyodorovitch was coming. She was watching out for you.”

“My darling mamma, that wasn’t at all clever of you. But if you want to make up for it by saying something very clever, dear mamma, then tell our honored guest, Alexey Fyodorovitch, that he has shown how witless he is by daring to come to us after what happened yesterday, when everyone is laughing at him.”

“Lise, you’re going too far. I swear I’ll have to be stern with you. Who is laughing at him? I’m so glad he’s come, I need him, I can’t do without him. Oh, Alexey Fyodorovitch, I am dreadfully unhappy!”
“But what’s wrong with you, mamma, darling?”

“Ah, your whims, Lise, your restlessness, your illness, that awful night of fever, that awful, everlasting Herzenstube, everlasting, everlasting, that’s the worst of it! Everything, in fact, everything.... Even that miracle, too! Oh, how it has upset me, how it has shattered me, that miracle, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch! And that tragedy in the drawing room, it’s more than I can bear, I warn you. I can’t bear it. A comedy, maybe, not a tragedy. Tell me, will Father Zossima live till tomorrow, will he? Oh, my God! What is happening to me? Every minute I close my eyes and see that it’s all nonsense, all nonsense.”
“I’d be very grateful,” Alyosha broke in suddenly, “if you could give me a clean rag to bandage my finger. I’ve hurt it, and it’s very painful.”
Alyosha undid the handkerchief around his bitten finger. It was soaked with blood. Madame Hohlakov screamed and shut her eyes.
“Good heavens, what a wound, how awful!”
But the moment Lise saw Alyosha’s finger through the crack, she threw the door wide open.

“Come in, come in here,” she cried, in a commanding voice. “No more nonsense! Good heavens, why did you just stand there all this time and say nothing about it? He could have bled to death, mamma! How did you do it? Water, water! First of all you must wash it, just hold it in cold water to stop the pain, and keep it there, keep it there.... Hurry, mamma, bring some water in a slop basin. But do hurry,” she finished nervously. The sight of Alyosha’s wound had given her a real fright.
“Shouldn’t we send for Herzenstube?” cried Madame Hohlakov.

“Mamma, you’ll be the death of me. Your Herzenstube will come and say he can make nothing of it! Water, water! Mamma, for goodness’ sake go yourself and hurry Yulia, she’s such a slowpoke, she never can come fast! Hurry, mamma, or I’ll die.”
“Really, it’s nothing much,” cried Alyosha, alarmed by all this alarm.
Yulia ran in with water, and Alyosha put his finger into it.

“Some lint, mamma, for mercy’s sake, bring some lint and that muddy lotion for wounds, what’s it called? We have some. You know where the bottle is, mamma; it’s in your bedroom, in the right-hand cupboard, there’s a big bottle of it there with the lint.”
“I’ll bring everything in a minute, Lise, only don’t scream and don’t make a fuss. You see how bravely Alexey Fyodorovitch bears it. Where did you get such a dreadful wound, Alexey Fyodorovitch?”
Madame Hohlakov hurried off. This was just what Lise had been waiting for.
“First of all, answer my question: where did you get hurt like this?” she asked Alyosha quickly. “And then I’ll talk to you about something quite different. Well?”

Alyosha sensed that the time while her mother was out of the room was precious to her. So he hurried to tell her, in as few words as possible, about his puzzling encounter with the schoolboys. Lise clasped her hands as she listened.

“How can you mix with schoolboys, and dressed like that, too?” she cried angrily, as though she had a right to tell him what to do. “If you can do that, you’re nothing but a boy yourself, a perfect boy! But you must find out about that horrid boy for me and tell me everything, because there’s some mystery in it. Now for the second thing, but first a question: does the pain stop you from talking about utterly unimportant things, but talking sensibly?”
“Of course not, and it doesn’t hurt much now.”

“That’s only because your finger is in the water. We’ll have to change it very soon, because it will get warm in a minute. Yulia, bring some ice from the cellar and another basin of water. Now that she’s gone I can speak; will you give me the letter I sent you yesterday, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch—be quick, because mamma will be back any minute and I don’t want—”
“I don’t have the letter.”
“That’s not true, you do. I knew you’d say that. It’s in that pocket. I’ve been sorry about that joke all night. Give me the letter back this minute, give it to me.”
“I left it at home.”

“But you can’t treat me like a child, a little girl, after that silly joke! I’m sorry for being so silly, but you must bring me the letter, if you really haven’t got it with you—bring it today, you must, you must.”
“I can’t possibly today, because I’m going back to the monastery, and I won’t be able to come and see you for the next two days—three or four, maybe—because Father Zossima—”
“Four days, what nonsense! Listen. Did you laugh at me a lot?”
“I didn’t laugh at all.”
“Why not?”
“Because I believed everything you wrote.”
“You’re insulting me!”

“Not at all. As soon as I read it, I thought all of it would come true, because as soon as Father Zossima dies, I have to leave the monastery. Then I’ll go back to my studies and finish them, and when you come of age we’ll be married. I’ll love you. I haven’t had time to think about it, but I don’t believe I could find a better wife than you, and Father Zossima tells me I must marry.”
“But I’m a cripple, wheeled about in a chair,” laughed Lise, her face flushing crimson.
“I’ll wheel you around myself, but I’m sure you’ll be well by then.”

“But you’re mad,” said Lise nervously, “to make all this nonsense out of a joke! And here’s mamma, perhaps just in time, _à propos_. Mamma, you’re always so slow, how can you be so long! And here’s Yulia with the ice!”

“Oh, Lise, don’t scream, above all, don’t scream. That screaming drives me ... What am I supposed to do when you put the lint somewhere else? I’ve been hunting and hunting—I do believe you did it on purpose.”
“But how could I know he’d turn up with a bad finger? Otherwise perhaps I really would have done it on purpose. My darling mamma, you’re starting to say truly witty things.”

“Never mind whether I’m witty, but I must say you’re showing a lovely feeling for Alexey Fyodorovitch’s suffering! Oh, my dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, what’s killing me isn’t any single thing, not Herzenstube, but everything all together, that’s what’s too much for me.”

“That’s enough, mamma, enough about Herzenstube,” Lise laughed merrily. “Hurry up with the lint and the lotion, mamma. That’s only Goulard’s water, Alexey Fyodorovitch, I’ve remembered the name now, but it’s a splendid lotion. Would you believe it, mamma, on his way here he got into a fight with some boys in the street, and one of them bit his finger. Isn’t he a child, a child himself? Is he fit to marry after that? Because just imagine, mamma, he wants to be married. Just think of him married, wouldn’t it be funny, wouldn’t it be awful?”
And Lise kept on laughing her thin, hysterical giggle, glancing slyly at Alyosha.
“But why married, Lise? What makes you talk about such a thing? It’s quite out of place—and perhaps that boy was rabid.”
“Oh, mamma! As if there were rabid boys!”

“Why not, Lise, as though I’d said something stupid! Your boy might have been bitten by a mad dog, and then he’d go mad and bite anyone near him. How well she has bandaged it, Alexey Fyodorovitch! I couldn’t have done it. Does it still hurt?”
“It’s nothing much now.”
“You aren’t afraid of water?” asked Lise.

“Come now, that’s enough, Lise, perhaps I really was a little too quick to talk about the boy being rabid, and you jumped on it right away. Katerina Ivanovna has only just heard that you’re here, Alexey Fyodorovitch, she simply rushed at me, she’s dying to see you, dying!”
“Ach, mamma, go to them yourself. He can’t go just now, he’s in too much pain.”
“Not at all, I can go perfectly well,” said Alyosha.
“What! You’re going away? Is that what you’re saying?”

“Well, once I’ve seen them, I’ll come back here and we can talk as much as you like. But I’d like to see Katerina Ivanovna right now, because I’m very anxious to get back to the monastery as soon as I can.”
“Mamma, take him away quickly. Alexey Fyodorovitch, don’t bother coming to see me afterwards, just go straight back to your monastery, and good riddance. I want to sleep, I didn’t sleep all night.”
“Ah, Lise, you’re only teasing, but how I wish you would sleep!” cried Madame Hohlakov.
“I don’t know what I’ve done.... I’ll stay another three minutes, or five if you like,” muttered Alyosha.
“Even five! Do take him away quickly, mamma, he’s a monster.”

“Lise, you’re out of your mind. Let’s go, Alexey Fyodorovitch, she’s too capricious today. I’m afraid to cross her. Oh, the trouble you have with nervous girls! Perhaps she really will be able to sleep after seeing you. How quickly you’ve made her sleepy, and how lucky that is!”
“Ah, mamma, how sweetly you talk! I must kiss you for that, mamma.”

“And I kiss you too, Lise. Listen, Alexey Fyodorovitch,” Madame Hohlakov began, mysteriously and importantly, in a quick whisper. “I don’t want to hint at anything, I don’t want to lift the veil, you’ll see for yourself what’s going on. It’s appalling. It’s the most fantastic farce. She loves your brother Ivan, and she’s doing everything she can to convince herself that she loves your brother Dmitri. It’s appalling! I’ll go in with you, and if they don’t throw me out, I’ll stay to the end.”
